newsitem.title: NORWAY: FEATURE - Former U.N. mediator bitter at U.S. role in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Former U.N. mediator bitter at U.S. role in Bosnia.

text.p: Thorvald Stoltenberg, the former U.N. mediator for ex-Yugoslavia, blames Washington for the inability of the West to impose an early peace in Bosnia.
In his book "The Thousand Days", the 65-year-old Norwegian diplomat is preoccupied with the United States and its insistence on staying on the sidelines at the beginning of the four-year Bosnian war.

Looking back over his two-and-a-half years working with European Union mediator Lord David Owen to negotiate an end to the conflict, Stoltenberg writes that it could have been stopped in late 1993 if the United States had given its backing.
"The biggest difference between the (1995) Dayton agreement and the agreement from December 1993 is to be found in the cemeteries and the refugee camps," his book says bitterly.

The Dayton treaty was negotiated by U.S. mediator Richard Holbrooke as assistant secretary of state after Washington moved in to solve the conflict in 1995 and NATO subsequently sent in thousands of peacekeeping troops.

"I belonged to those who for a long time tried to get the United States more strongly involved in the negotiating process," Stoltenberg says. "I am happy that Washington finally changed politics and committed itself all-out. But this should have happened much earlier."
U.S. POLICY "HELD UP PEACE DEAL"

Holbrooke has been hailed as a hero. But Stoltenberg disagrees with the view, widely voiced in the United States, that the United Nations and the EU had failed in Bosnia and that the outnumbered U.N. peacekeepers had been hapless figures.

Like Owen in a book last year, Stoltenberg suggests that a Bosnian peace deal agreed by Serbs, Croats and the Moslem-led government in Sarajevo in late 1993 collapsed because Washington did not back it.

"Think of how much destruction and suffering could have been spared if everyone had shown the same resolve and strength in 1993 as in 1995?" he says in the 400-page book, which will soon be translated into English and Serbo-Croatian.
Some diplomats say U.S. officials in 1993 pushed the Moslems to pull out by signalling Washington might come to their help or at least ensure they were supplied with better weaponry.

Stoltenberg says the Moslems arguably had a better deal under the 1993 peace plan because they would have received 33.3 percent of Bosnia's land. Under Dayton, they ended up with around 30 percent, he says.
One shift in the U.S. position was that Washington started talking to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, he says.

"Now Washington committed itself fully to Milosevic. To the Americans he had primarily been the man who started the war. He was supposed to be pressured and isolated. Now it was him that they trusted," Stoltenberg writes.

He says Milosevic, a former banker, came across neither as a Serb nationalist nor the convinced communist he had earlier appeared to be. He was a useful counter-partner in the talks because he called the shots in the Serb camp and could put pressure on the Bosnian Serbs.
"He was analytical and interesting and spoke with determination and persuasion, although he was not always careful with facts. But that was true for all the (Balkan) leaders."
ESCAPING A "SEA OF SUFFERING"
Stoltenberg spent time negotiating with Radovan Karadzic, a former psychiatrist who eventually stepped down as Bosnian Serb president in July under international pressure.

The U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague has charged Karadzic with crimes against humanity and genocide linked to the siege of Sarajevo, the capture of U.N. peacekeepers and the slaughter of up to 8,000 Moslem men from the Srebrenica enclave.
"He liked speaking at length about the destiny of the Serbs," Stoltenberg recalls. "He was convinced that he was doing the West a favour by fighting Moslems in Bosnia.

"It was difficult to negotiate with Karadzic. He had a dubious relation with facts, to put it mildly. He seemed nervous and he changed his mind all the time. It appeared that he did not trust anyone, not even his Bosnian Serb colleagues. But nobody could deny he knew the country well."
Stoltenberg says Croatian President Franjo Tudjman was a man of pomp and circumstance. A meeting with him, in his palace guarded by soldiers in red uniforms, was always a formal affair.

"Tudjman's view of Milosevic had two sides. On the one hand the Serb president was the devil himself -- a picture Tudjman liked to invoke in public statements. At the same time he admired Milosevic. Tudjman wanted to come across as an equal to the Serb leader."
Bosnian Moslem President Alija Izetbegovic often resembled a jovial grandfather "but in meetings and around the negotiating table he sometimes seemed torn and tired," Stoltenberg says.
"It was fully understandable. The other presidents did not live in a city (Sarajevo) that was under fire practically every day."
Stoltenberg, a former foreign minister, became Norway's ambassador to Copenhagen after his peace mission ended a year ago. He is happy with the switch.

"I am pleased to have a job now that does not almost every day bring bad news or troubles, a job where I don't have to go to bed every night with a feeling of being powerless before a sea of suffering, a job where I do not every day deal with broken promises, intrigues and, at best, half-truths.
"The thousand days are over. But the trace of them will mark every day of the rest of my life."
